title: The Attributes of God
subtitle: Aseity, simplicity, omniscience, omnipresence, omnipotence, immutability, goodness. Classical theism, and the questions pressed against it.
triageNote: The core attributes are not optional features of God you may take or leave. That God is all-knowing, all-powerful, present everywhere, good, and dependent on nothing is the God of Scripture. It is the God the church has always confessed. Deny that God knows all things or is good, and you are no longer talking about the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. So the central claim of this page, that God is the infinite, perfect, self-existent being Scripture reveals, is first-order. What runs lower is the in-house argument over how to hold certain attributes together. Whether divine simplicity is strict or softened. How omniscience relates to human freedom. Whether immutability allows God real responsiveness. Those are real debates among the orthodox, marked where they come. Hold the attributes themselves with your life. Hold the philosophical models with care.
question: When Scripture says God is, what kind of being is being claimed. Not a very large, very old, very powerful version of us, a man writ cosmic. The God of the Bible is of a different order entirely. He depends on nothing, exists from himself, knows all that can be known. He is present everywhere without being contained anywhere. He can do all that power can do. He does not change in his being or character. And he is good without measure and without shadow. The classical tradition gathered these into a set of perfections and gave them names. Aseity, that God is from himself. Simplicity, that God is not composed of parts. Omniscience, omnipresence, omnipotence. Immutability, that God does not change. And the moral perfections, that God is holy, just, faithful, and good. The question this page asks is what each of these means, how strongly the tradition meant them, and where the hardest pressure falls. Because each perfection, pushed, raises a real question. If God cannot change, can he love, respond, grieve. If God knows everything, am I free. If God can do anything, why is there evil. The attributes are not a list to memorize. They are a portrait. And the portrait has edges that have been argued over for centuries.
whyItMatters:
Your picture of God's attributes is the foundation under everything else you believe, whether you have ever stated it or not. If you secretly think God is powerful but not quite good, you will obey him from fear and never trust him. If you think he is good but not quite powerful, you will love him and quietly despair. A good God who cannot help you is a tragedy, not a refuge. The whole Christian life runs on holding the perfections together. A God good enough to want your good and strong enough to secure it. Knowing enough to never be surprised by your trouble, present enough to be with you in it. Strip out any one attribute and the others curdle.

It also decides whether God is a refuge or a rival. A great deal of modern unbelief is really a complaint against a misdrawn portrait. A God who is mostly power and surveillance, a cosmic watcher who knows everything and judges everything and is impossible to love. But the classical attributes, rightly seen, are not threats. That God knows all things means he knows you to the bottom and has not turned away. That God is present everywhere means there is no pit you can fall into where he is not already waiting. That God does not change means his love for you is not subject to his moods or yours. The attributes you might first hear as cold are, when you live inside them, the only solid ground there is.

And the attributes are where doubt does its real work. People rarely lose their faith over a doctrine of the church. They lose it at the place where an attribute seems to collide with their life. A good God and a dead child. An all-knowing God and my own freedom. An unchanging God and a Bible full of God seeming to relent. The honest way to hold the attributes is to feel that pressure, not to wave it off. And to know which questions the tradition has answered and which it has only learned to live with. This page tries to do both.

positions.name: Classical theism: God as the perfect, simple, self-existent being
positions.inOneLine: God is pure being, dependent on nothing, without parts, knowing and present and powerful without limit, unchanging in essence and character, and good without measure. The attributes are not pieces of God but the one infinite God seen from different angles.
positions.bestCase:
Let me start where the tradition starts, with the burning bush, because everything else unfolds from it. Moses asks for God's name, and God answers, I am who I am. Not I am your tribal deity, not I am the strongest of the gods, but I am. God names himself as sheer being, the one who simply is. He needs nothing outside himself to exist or to be what he is. This is aseity, from the Latin a se, from himself. Everything else that exists is derived, contingent, hangs by a thread over nonexistence. God alone exists of himself. That single fact reorders the universe. He did not need to create. He gains nothing from your worship and loses nothing from your rebellion. That is precisely why his love for you is pure gift and not transaction. The God who needs you would use you. The God who needs nothing can simply love you.

From aseity flows simplicity, the most misunderstood of the perfections, so let me state it plainly. Simplicity means God is not composed of parts. He is not made of his attributes the way a wall is made of bricks. You cannot take goodness and power and knowledge and stack them up to get God. Rather, God is his attributes. His justice is his mercy is his power is his being. One infinite perfection that our small minds can only grasp by looking at it from different sides and giving each side a name. This is why Scripture does not say God has love but God is love. The point of simplicity is not abstraction. There is no part of God at war with another part. No chance that his mercy might one day be overruled by his justice. No hidden God behind the God you have met. What you see in Christ is not a department of God. It is God.

Now the great perfections, quickly, because the tradition holds them as one. Omniscience: God knows all things, actual and possible, in one eternal act. He does not learn or infer. All things stand open before him, including the secrets of your heart. Omnipresence: God is wholly present everywhere. He is not spread thin like a gas filling a room but present in his whole being at every point, nearer to you than you are to yourself, as Augustine said. Omnipotence: God can do all that power can do, all that is not a contradiction in terms. That is no limit on God. A square circle is not a thing power could make. It is nonsense wearing the costume of a sentence. Immutability: God does not change in his being or his character. The God who is already infinite perfection cannot improve, for there is nothing higher to grow into. And he cannot decay, for nothing can diminish him. Malachi says it: I the Lord do not change.

And then the moral perfections crown the rest. God is holy, set apart in blazing purity. God is just, never doing wrong, never overlooking it. God is faithful, true to every word. And God is good, the source and standard of all good. He is not good by measuring up to a goodness above him but good as the very definition of the word. Hold these together and you have the God of Scripture. Infinite, perfect, self-existent, bent toward his creatures in love that costs him nothing to give and everything to give well. This is the God the church has worshiped. I think the reason the attributes can frighten a modern reader is that we have shrunk God to our size and then found the full-sized God overwhelming. Let him be God, and the perfections stop being threats and become the firmest ground there is.
advocates: modern defenders such as Stephen Charnock and James Dolezal

positions.name: Theistic personalism, or relational theism: the perfections held more flexibly
positions.inOneLine: God has all the great-making attributes to the highest degree, but is best understood as the supreme personal being who genuinely knows, acts, and responds in time. Strict simplicity and a timeless immutability obscure the living, responsive God of the biblical narrative.
positions.bestCase:
I hold every attribute the classical tradition names. God is supreme in power, knowledge, presence, and goodness, dependent on nothing, the maker of all that is. Hear that clearly before you hear my worry. My worry is that the classical tradition, in its zeal to make God absolutely unlike creatures, borrowed a frame from Greek philosophy. The frame quietly muffles the God who actually appears in Scripture, the God who speaks, hears, relents, rejoices, and grieves.

Take simplicity, in its strict form. The claim that God is identical with each of his attributes, that his mercy just is his justice with no distinction in God at all, strains against the plain way Scripture speaks. There God's anger and his compassion are really different and really interact. There mercy triumphs over judgment. I would rather say God has these perfections, all of them, perfectly and without conflict. The alternative collapses them into a single undifferentiated point that no longer answers to the rich personal portrait of the Bible. Strict simplicity, pressed, makes God so unlike a person that it becomes hard to say he loves you in any sense you would recognize as love.

Take immutability, in its strongest form, joined to timeless eternity. The classical claim that God is utterly outside time and cannot change in any respect runs hard against a Bible in which God responds. Hezekiah prays and God adds fifteen years. God says he relents over the disaster he had planned for Nineveh. The tradition explains these as accommodations, figures of speech, the unchanging God described as if he changed for our benefit. But there are an awful lot of them. At some point the explanation starts to feel like a system protecting itself from its own Bible. I would rather say God is unchanging in his character and his promises, absolutely faithful, never capricious. But genuinely responsive within his relationship to a world he made to be real. A God who cannot be moved by his children is not greater than a God who can. He is colder.

What am I guarding. The living God. The God of the burning bush is also the God who says, I have surely seen the affliction of my people, and I have heard their cry, and I have come down. Seen, heard, come down. I will not let a philosophical commitment to absolute changelessness turn those verbs into mere appearances. I affirm aseity, I affirm omniscience and omnipotence, I deny nothing that makes God God. I only insist that the supreme being is supremely personal. A doctrine of the attributes which cannot account for a God who relates, responds, and feels has purchased its consistency at a price. The price is the God who is actually there.
advocates: William Lane Craig (in a moderated form)

biblicalEvidence.summary: God names himself to Moses: I am who I am. The classical tradition reads this as God revealing himself as sheer being, the self-existent one who depends on nothing. It is the foundation of aseity and of the whole doctrine of the attributes.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that makes God one being among others, however supreme. The name claims a wholly underived existence.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical theism takes I am as the disclosure of God's pure being and aseity, the ground of every other perfection. Relational theists agree God is self-existent but read the name more as a promise of covenant presence, I will be who I will be, I will be there for you. They stress the relational and forward-looking sense alongside the metaphysical one.

biblicalEvidence.summary: For I the Lord do not change; therefore you, O children of Jacob, are not consumed. God's unchangeableness is given as the reason his people are not destroyed. Because he does not change, his covenant promise holds.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that makes God's character or purpose genuinely alterable. Here his not changing is the ground of Israel's survival.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical theism reads this as immutability in the full sense, God's being and character beyond all change. Relational theists note that the verse grounds immutability specifically in God's covenant faithfulness, his promises do not change. They read it as constancy of character and commitment rather than a denial that God ever responds within his dealings with the world.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Classical theism, on omniscience and omnipresence
biblicalEvidence.summary: O Lord, you have searched me and known me. You discern my thoughts from afar. Where shall I flee from your presence? The psalm presents God knowing the psalmist completely and present in every place. From heaven to Sheol to the far side of the sea.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that limits God's knowledge or presence. The psalm extends both to every place and every thought, before a word is on the tongue.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All views affirm this as a high statement of omniscience and omnipresence. Classical theism reads it as exhaustive knowledge held in one eternal act. Those who limit foreknowledge of free future choices (see the foreknowledge page) still affirm this knowledge of the present and past. The contested point there is future free acts, not the searching knowledge the psalm celebrates.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The God who made the world does not live in temples made by man, nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. Paul tells the Athenians that God needs nothing from his creatures.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that makes God dependent on the world or enriched by it. Paul denies that God needs anything, naming aseity directly.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical theism takes this as a clear statement of divine aseity and self-sufficiency. Relational theists agree God needs nothing for his existence or perfection, while distinguishing need from genuine relationship. That God depends on nothing does not, they argue, mean God cannot truly delight in or be moved by what he freely made.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Relational theism, pressed against strict immutability
biblicalEvidence.summary: And the Lord regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart. Before the flood, God is said to regret and to be grieved. Language of real emotion and apparent change of mind.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for strict immutability and impassibility. God is said to regret and to grieve, which sound like change and feeling in God.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical theism reads this as anthropopathism, Scripture describing God in human terms so we can grasp his settled opposition to sin. It is not a literal change in the changeless God. Relational theists answer that the explanation is invoked so often it begins to explain away the text. They take the grief as a real, if perfectly holy, divine response. The impassibility page takes this question up directly.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Relational theism, pressed against strict immutability
biblicalEvidence.summary: When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it. Nineveh repents, and God relents.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that denies God ever responds to what creatures do. The text makes God's relenting a response to Nineveh's repentance.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical theism reads God's relenting as the unchanging God's consistent character meeting changed creatures. He always pardons the penitent, so what changes is Nineveh, not God. His stated threat was the warning that produced the repentance. Relational theists take the relenting at closer to face value, as God's genuine, contingent response within a real relationship. They point to Jeremiah 18 where God states this responsiveness as a principle of how he deals with nations.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The Lord is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable. God is presented as inexhaustible in power and beyond the limits of created understanding.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that scales God down toward the creaturely. His power does not tire and his understanding cannot be searched out.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All views affirm this. Classical theism reads it as a statement of God's infinite, unwearying perfection, the Creator categorically above the creature. Relational theists affirm the same inexhaustibility while holding that God's choice to engage his creation in time is not weakness. It is the free act of this infinite God.

biblicalEvidence.summary: God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. The moral perfection of God, his holiness and goodness, stated without qualification. No shadow, no hidden dark side, no part of God at odds with his goodness.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that imagines a hidden, arbitrary, or partly malevolent God behind the God revealed in Christ. There is no darkness in him at all.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical theism reads this together with simplicity. Because God is not composed of parts, there is no dark part, his goodness is his very being. Relational theists read it as the moral purity of the personal God who is wholly good in all his dealings. Both take it as ruling out any God behind the back of the God revealed in Jesus.

weighing:
My judgment, given quietly, one reader to another, and held loosely where the tradition itself has held things loosely.

I stand with classical theism. I want to say why before I say where I feel the pressure. The attributes, as the great tradition drew them, hang together with a beauty that the looser accounts never quite recover. Aseity is the keystone. Once you see that God exists from himself and needs nothing, every other perfection falls into place. More than that, the gospel itself comes into focus. A God who needs nothing loves you for no reason but love. That is the only love worth having. And simplicity, far from being cold abstraction, is the guarantee I most need. There is no hidden God behind the God of the cross. No department of justice waiting to overrule the mercy I have met in Christ. When I am afraid, the classical attributes are not the problem. They are the cure.

Where I feel the pressure, honestly, is exactly where the relational theists press. The sheer number of texts in which God sees, hears, relents, grieves, and responds. The classical answer, that these are accommodations, God described as if he changed so that we can understand his unchanging character, is right as far as it goes. And I think it is right. But I will not pretend it costs nothing. Nor that a sensitive reader does not sometimes feel the system straining to keep its Bible from speaking too plainly. My own resolution, tentative, is that the tradition is correct that God's being and character do not change and do not improve. Infinite perfection has nowhere to go. But I want to hold that with enough warmth to take seriously that the God who does not change is also the God who came down. He was moved with compassion. He wept at a grave. The changelessness is the changelessness of a love that will not cool, not the stillness of a stone.

So I land here. The core attributes, first-order, the God of Scripture, not up for negotiation. The strict-versus-softened debate over simplicity and immutability is a real and serious in-house argument. I lean classical while granting the relational theists have named a pressure the classical account must keep feeling and not explain away. Let the perfections be as large as Scripture makes them. Let the largeness drive you to worship rather than to fear.
charitableDisagreement:
Watch the line carefully here, because two different things sit on this page. That God is all-knowing, all-powerful, present everywhere, self-existent, and good is first-order. Someone who denies that God is good, or makes him finite and struggling and unsure of the future in the way a creature is, has changed the subject. They are no longer speaking of the God of Scripture but of a lesser thing. Clarity there is not arrogance, it is faithfulness. The church owes its people a God big enough to trust.

But the argument between strict classical theism and the more relational accounts is a different matter. It runs between people who both worship the infinite God and both read the same Bible. If you hold the classical view, as I do, do not treat every relational theist as a heretic smuggling a small god into the church. The best of them are guarding the living, responsive God of the narrative against a frozen abstraction. That is a real danger and not an imaginary one. If you hold the relational view, do not treat the classical tradition's commitment to simplicity and immutability as cold philosophy that has lost the Bible. It is the hard-won grammar that keeps God from being a part-God at war with himself, with a hidden dark side behind the cross.

So, is it a hill to die on. The attributes themselves, yes, defend them with everything. A shrunken God cannot save and cannot be trusted. The fine print, the precise model of simplicity, the exact sense of immutability, no. That is a conversation the faithful have always had inside the same worship. Confess the infinite, perfect, self-existent God without flinching. Argue the philosophical models with the humility of a creature trying to think about the One whose understanding is unsearchable.

relatedDebates.topic: Does God suffer? Impassibility and its rivals
relatedDebates.note: If God is immutable, can he feel grief, or be moved by his creatures' pain. The doctrine of impassibility holds that God does not suffer as creatures do. Passibilism holds that the God of the cross genuinely suffers with and for the world. This is the sharpest edge of the immutability debate. The impassibility page takes it up on its own terms.

relatedDebates.topic: Omniscience and the freedom of the creature
relatedDebates.note: If God knows everything, including every choice you will ever make, in what sense are you free. And can God change his mind in answer to prayer. Classical theism, open theism, and Molinism give different answers, each holding omniscience and freedom together in a different way. The foreknowledge page maps that debate.

Whether God is strictly identical with each of his attributes, with no real distinction among them, or whether the attributes are really distinct perfections held without conflict. That is one of the oldest questions in the doctrine of God. It bears on how we read every other attribute. Simplicity is the claim that the attributes are finally one in the one God.
